lines.text: The oldest gold, the birthplace of an alphabet, and five centuries under the Ottomans. This is the story of Bulgaria, from Thrace to the euro.
More than six thousand years ago, near Varna on the Black Sea, people were buried with the oldest worked gold in the world.
Later the Thracians ruled these lands, and at Kazanlak a tomb was painted with scenes that still glow today.
In the seventh century Khan Asparuh led the Bulgars to the Danube, and in 681 he founded a state.
So began the First Bulgarian Empire, which would last more than three centuries.
Under Tsar Simeon the first, it reached its golden age, a rival to Byzantium itself.
Around this time, in Bulgaria, the Cyrillic alphabet was created, now used by many millions of people.
In 946 the Rila Monastery was founded in the mountains, and it became the heart of Bulgarian faith.
Tsar Samuel fought Byzantium for decades, until 1014, when his captured army was blinded.
Bulgaria fell, but in 1185 it rose again as the Second Empire, until the Ottomans came.
Five hundred years of Ottoman rule followed. In 1837 Vasil Levski was born, who would organise the fight for freedom and be hanged for it.
In 1850 Ivan Vazov was born, the writer of Under the Yoke, the great novel of Bulgaria's struggle.
In April 1876 Bulgarians rose against Ottoman rule. The rising was put down with terrible force.
A year later Russia went to war with the Ottomans, and the war set Bulgaria free.
In 1878 a free Bulgaria was born again, on the land where its alphabet was made.
In Sofia, work began on the great Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, in honour of the Russians who died for its freedom.
In 1911 Todor Zhivkov was born, the communist who would rule Bulgaria for thirty-five years.
In 1943, during the Second World War, protests by ordinary Bulgarians stopped the deportation of the country's forty-eight thousand Jews.
In 1966 Hristo Stoichkov was born, who led Bulgaria to fourth place at the 1994 World Cup.
After the fall of communism, in 2007 Bulgaria joined the European Union, alongside Romania.
And on the first of January 2026, Bulgaria adopted the euro.
From Thracian gold to the euro, Bulgaria has kept its alphabet and its spirit.
